claim: Mitochondria are maternally inherited in most animals, including mammals.
source: In most animals, including mammals, mitochondria are inherited strictly through the maternal lineage.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial inheritance patterns.

claim: Sperm deliver mitochondria into the egg during fertilization.
source: Because sperm deliver mitochondria into the egg during fertilization, mechanisms likely exist to eliminate paternal mitochondria from the early embryo.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about fertilization.

claim: Uniparental inheritance of mitochondria ensures that only one haplotype of mitochondrial DNA exists in the offspring.
source: Uniparental inheritance of mitochondria ensures that only one haplotype of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) exists in the offspring, a phenomenon with considerable biomedical implications.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of uniparental inheritance and is established knowledge.

claim: Maternal inheritance of mitochondria underlies the maternal inheritance of diseases caused by mutations in mtDNA.
source: It underlies the maternal inheritance of diseases caused by mutations in mtDNA (Carelli and Chan, 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Carelli and Chan, 2014.

claim: Maternal inheritance of mitochondria enables the use of mtDNA sequences to track human migrations during evolution.
source: and enables the use of mtDNA sequences to track human migrations during evolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge in evolutionary biology.

claim: Extensive heteroplasmy is genetically unstable and associated with physiological abnormalities in mice.
source: Mouse studies suggest that extensive heteroplasmy, the co-existence of more than one haplotype of mtDNA, is genetically unstable and associated with physiological abnormalities (Sharpley et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sharpley et al., 2012.

claim: Paternal mitochondria are eliminated by mitophagy in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: The phenomenon has been most decisively dissected in Caenorhabditis elegans, where paternal mitochondria are eliminated by mitophagy (Al Rawi et al., 2011; Sato and Sato, 2011; Zhou et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Al Rawi et al., 2011; Sato and Sato, 2011; Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Mitophagy is a process in which mitochondria are engulfed by autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for destruction.
source: where paternal mitochondria are eliminated by mitophagy (Al Rawi et al., 2011; Sato and Sato, 2011; Zhou et al., 2011), a process in which mitochondria are engulfed by autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for destruction.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, paternal mitochondrial elimination involves autophagic components but occurs independently of PARKIN.
source: In Drosophila melanogaster, paternal mitochondrial elimination involves autophagic components but occurs independently of PARKIN (Politi et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to Politi et al., 2014.

claim: PARKIN is a Parkinson's disease-related E3 ubiquitin ligase that is central to the most heavily studied mitophagy pathway.
source: a Parkinson's disease-related E3 ubiquitin ligase that is central to the most heavily studied mitophagy pathway (Pickrell and Youle, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pickrell and Youle, 2015.

claim: Sperm mitochondria from mice are ubiquitinated.
source: Consistent with a role for autophagy, sperm mitochondria from mice are ubiquitinated (Sutovsky et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sutovsky et al., 1999.

claim: After fertilization, sperm mitochondria are immuno-positive for P62 and the ATG8 homologs LC3 and GABARAP.
source: and, after fertilization, are immuno-positive for P62 and the ATG8 homologs LC3 and GABARAP (Al Rawi et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Al Rawi et al., 2011.

claim: A study disputed the role of autophagy in elimination of paternal mitochondria in mouse.
source: However, a subsequent study in mouse disputed the role of autophagy in elimination of paternal mitochondria (Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2013.

claim: The association of LC3 with paternal mitochondria is transient and occurs well before paternal mitochondrial elimination.
source: The association of LC3 with paternal mitochondria was observed to be transient and occurred well before paternal mitochondrial elimination.
evidence: This is a finding from Luo et al., 2013 as described in the text.

claim: Paternal mitochondria are segregated unevenly to blastomeres during early embryonic cell division.
source: In addition, it was found that paternal mitochondria were segregated unevenly to blastomeres during early embryonic cell division.
evidence: This is a finding from Luo et al., 2013 as described in the text.

claim: Luo et al. (2013) advocated a passive dilution mechanism whereby murine paternal mitochondria are stochastically lost due to uneven segregation to the cells of the embryo.
source: Based on these results, the authors rejected the role of autophagy and advocated a passive dilution mechanism whereby murine paternal mitochondria are stochastically lost due to uneven segregation to the cells of the embryo (Luo et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2013.

claim: In C. elegans, paternal mitochondria persist in embryos depleted for core autophagy genes such as LGG-1 and LGG-2.
source: In C. elegans, the functional role of autophagy was revealed by the persistence of paternal mitochondria in embryos depleted for core autophagy genes, such as the ATG8 homologs LGG-1 and LGG-2 (Al Rawi et al., 2011; Sato and Sato, 2011; Zhou et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Al Rawi et al., 2011; Sato and Sato, 2011; Zhou et al., 2011.

claim: Disruption of basal autophagy results in embryonic arrest at the four-cell stage in mouse.
source: A similar approach is not feasible in mouse, however, because disruption of basal autophagy results in embryonic arrest at the four-cell stage (Tsukamoto et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Tsukamoto et al., 2008.

claim: Cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos use a common pathway for elimination of mitochondria.
source: Here, we show that cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos use a common pathway for elimination of mitochondria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both cultured mouse fibroblasts and pre-implantation embryos utilize mitophagy for elimination of mitochondria.
source: Both situations utilize mitophagy, in which mitochondria are sequestered by autophagosomes and delivered to lysosomes for degradation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The E3 ubiquitin ligases PARKIN and MUL1 play redundant roles in elimination of paternal mitochondria.
source: The E3 ubiquitin ligases PARKIN and MUL1 play redundant roles in elimination of paternal mitochondria.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elimination of paternal mitochondria is associated with depolarization of paternal mitochondria.
source: The process is associated with depolarization of paternal mitochondria
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elimination of paternal mitochondria requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1.
source: and additionally requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and PINK1 kinase.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elimination of paternal mitochondria requires the autophagy adaptor P62.
source: and additionally requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and PINK1 kinase.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elimination of paternal mitochondria requires PINK1 kinase.
source: and additionally requires the mitochondrial outer membrane protein FIS1, the autophagy adaptor P62, and PINK1 kinase.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Strict maternal transmission of mitochondria relies on mitophagy.
source: Our results indicate that strict maternal transmission of mitochondria relies on mitophagy
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MUL1 and PARKIN collaborate in the process of paternal mitochondrial elimination.
source: and uncover a collaboration between MUL1 and PARKIN in this process.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PhAM mice have all mitochondria labeled with a mitochondrially-targeted version of the photoconvertible Dendra2 fluorescent protein.
source: To develop an assay to track paternal mitochondria in the early mouse embryo, we utilized male PhAM mice, in which all mitochondria, including those in the sperm midpiece, are labeled with a mitochondrially-targeted version of the photoconvertible Dendra2 fluorescent protein (Pham et al., 2012) (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pham et al., 2012 and Figure 1A.

claim: When male PhAM mice are mated with wild-type females, the resulting embryos contain brightly fluorescent paternal mitochondria.
source: When male PhAM mice were mated with wild-type females, the resulting embryos contained brightly fluorescent paternal mitochondria.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: At 12 hr post-fertilization, paternal mitochondria are found in a linear cluster reflecting their original, compact organization in the sperm midpiece.
source: At 12 hr post-fertilization (Figure 1B), the paternal mitochondria were found in a linear cluster, reflecting their original, compact organization in the sperm midpiece.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1B.

claim: At 36 hr after fertilization, the paternal mitochondrial cluster begins to disperse in cultured embryos.
source: At 36 hr after fertilization (Figure 1C), this cluster began to disperse in cultured embryos, and thereafter, well-separated individual mitochondria were visible within blastomeres.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1C.

claim: Paternal mitochondrial content progressively decreases over 2 days following 36 hr post-fertilization.
source: Over the next 2 days, paternal mitochondrial content progressively decreased (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 1D-F.

claim: At 84 hr after fertilization, the majority of embryos have lost all paternal mitochondria.
source: At 84 hr after fertilization, the majority of embryos had lost all paternal mitochondria (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1F.

claim: There is a reproducible and progressive loss of paternal mitochondria between 60 and 84 hr post-fertilization.
source: Quantification of these results showed a reproducible and progressive loss of paternal mitochondria between 60 and 84 hr post-fertilization (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1G.

claim: There is no reduction in maternal mitochondrial content between 60 and 84 hr post-fertilization in embryos with fluorescent maternal mitochondria.
source: In these embryos, there was no reduction in the maternal mitochondrial content between 60 and 84 hr post-fertilization (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Embryos injected with shRNA against Atg3 show arrest at the four-cell stage.
source: In embryos injected with shRNA against Atg3 (Figure 1K), however, embryo development was arrested at the four-cell stage, consistent with a previous report using Atg5-null oocytes (Tsukamoto et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1K and citation to Tsukamoto et al., 2008.

claim: Embryos treated with bafilomycin show arrested embryonic development.
source: Similarly, treatment of embryos with bafilomycin, an autophagy inhibitor, arrested embryonic development (Figure 1L).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1L.

claim: Embryos treated with Atg3 shRNA or bafilomycin show persistence of paternal mitochondria at 84 hr.
source: In both cases, the treated embryos showed persistence of paternal mitochondria at 84 hr.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Embryos injected with lentivirus encoding shRNA against Parkin show loss of paternal mitochondria by 84 hr after fertilization.
source: We injected embryos with lentivirus encoding shRNA against Parkin (Park2), an E3 ubiquitin ligase that is central to the most studied pathway for mitopahgy (Durcan and Fon, 2015; Pickrell and Youle, 2015). Such embryos show loss of paternal mitochondria by 84 hr after fertilization, suggesting that the process occurs in the absence of PARKIN (Figure 1M).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 1M and citations.

claim: When mouse embryonic fibroblasts are cultured with 10 mM glucose, they show few red-only mitochondria.
source: When mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) were cultured with a moderate concentration (10 mM) of glucose, a condition in which their metabolism relies largely on glycolysis, they showed few red-only mitochondria (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2A.

claim: When MEFs are cultured for 4 days in OXPHOS-inducing medium, many cells exhibit numerous red puncta.
source: When cells were cultured for 4 days in this OXPHOS-inducing medium, many cells exhibited numerous red puncta (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2A.

claim: Glucose-free conditions promote increased turnover of mitochondria.
source: This observation is consistent with a study showing that glucose-free conditions promote increased turnover of mitochondria (Melser et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Melser et al., 2013.

claim: Atg3 knockout MEFs do not form red puncta under the OXPHOS-inducing condition.
source: Atg3 knockout MEFs did not form red puncta under the OXPHOS-inducing condition (Figure 2B–C)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 2B-C.

claim: Formation of red puncta is dependent on the core autophagy machinery.
source: indicating that formation of red puncta is dependent on the core autophagy machinery.
evidence: This is an inference from the Atg3 knockout experiment.

claim: The level of lipidated LC3 is elevated under OXPHOS-inducing conditions.
source: Consistent with this idea, the level of lipidated LC3, another core component of the autophagy pathway, was elevated (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Red-only puncta co-localize extensively with mTurquoise2-LC3B.
source: Moreover, the red-only puncta co-localized extensively with mTurquoise2-LC3B, suggesting that they represent mitochondrial contents within the autophagosome pathway (Figure 2E, arrows).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2E.

claim: A subset of red puncta co-localize with LAMP1.
source: In addition, a subset of the red puncta co-localize with LAMP1, likely indicating later intermediates that have progressed to lysosomes (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2F.

claim: In glycolytic medium, mTurquoise2-LC3B does not co-localize with mitochondria.
source: In contrast, in glycolytic medium, mTurquoise2-LC3B did not co-localize with mitochondria (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2E.

claim: P62 localizes to mitochondria only under the OXPHOS-inducing condition.
source: In addition, we found that p62 (SQSTM1), a protein implicated in autophagy (Pankiv et al., 2007) and mitophagy (Seibenhener et al., 2013), localized to mitochondria only under the OXPHOS-inducing condition (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 2G and citations.

claim: P62 localizes to both red punctate mitochondria and elongated yellow mitochondria under OXPHOS conditions.
source: Unlike LC3B and LAMP1, however, P62 was localized to both red punctate mitochondria and elongated yellow mitochondria.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: The OXPHOS-inducing condition results in an increase in mitophagy intermediates.
source: These results indicate that the OXPHOS-inducing condition results in an increase in mitophagy intermediates.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: MEFs deficient in mitochondrial fusion (Mfn1, Mfn2, Mfn-dm, Opa1) are competent for mitophagy.
source: MEFs deficient in mitochondrial fusion were competent for mitophagy.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Mfn-dm cells show substantial mitophagy even under glycolytic culture conditions.
source: In fact, Mfn-dm cells and Opa1-/- cells showed substantial mitophagy even under glycolytic culture conditions, consistent with the findings that mitochondrial fusion protects against mitophagy (Gomes et al., 2011; Rambold et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by citations to Gomes et al., 2011 and Rambold et al., 2011.

claim: Opa1-/- cells show substantial mitophagy even under glycolytic culture conditions.
source: In fact, Mfn-dm cells and Opa1-/- cells showed substantial mitophagy even under glycolytic culture conditions, consistent with the findings that mitochondrial fusion protects against mitophagy (Gomes et al., 2011; Rambold et al., 2011)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by citations to Gomes et al., 2011 and Rambold et al., 2011.

claim: Mitochondrial fusion protects against mitophagy.
source: consistent with the findings that mitochondrial fusion protects against mitophagy (Gomes et al., 2011; Rambold et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gomes et al., 2011 and Rambold et al., 2011.

claim: Mfn-dm cells have constitutive localization of Parkin to mitochondria.
source: and that Mfn-dm cells have constitutive localization of Parkin to mitochondria (Narendra et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Narendra et al., 2008.

claim: Drp1-/- cells show normal levels of mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions.
source: Among cell lines deficient in mitochondrial fission, Drp1-/- and Mff-/- cells showed normal levels of mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Mff-/- cells show normal levels of mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions.
source: Among cell lines deficient in mitochondrial fission, Drp1-/- and Mff-/- cells showed normal levels of mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 3A.

claim: Fis1-/- cells have dramatically reduced mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions.
source: In contrast, Fis1-/- cells had dramatically reduced mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions (Figure 3A–B)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 3A-B.

claim: Fis1-/- cells show failure of both LC3 and P62 to co-localize with mitochondria.
source: and a failure of both LC3 and P62 to co-localize with mitochondria (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 3C-D.

claim: FIS1 does not play a prominent role in mammalian mitochondrial fission.
source: Although FIS1 is a central player in yeast mitochondrial fission, it does not play a prominent role in mammalian mitochondrial fission (Losón et al., 2013; Otera et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Losón et al., 2013 and Otera et al., 2010.

claim: FIS1 and TBC1D15 are implicated in mitochondrial degradation, specifically in PARKIN-dependent mitophagy.
source: Instead, recent studies implicate FIS1 and its interacting protein TBC1D15 (Onoue et al., 2013) in mitochondrial degradation, specifically in PARKIN-dependent mitophagy (Shen et al., 2014; Yamano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Onoue et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2014; Yamano et al., 2014.

claim: Tbc1d15 knockdown efficiently blocks mitophagy.
source: Similar to Fis1 deletion, Tbc1d15 knockdown efficiently blocked mitophagy and decreased LC3 and p62 localization to mitochondria (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 3C-E.

claim: Tbc1d15 knockdown decreases LC3 and p62 localization to mitochondria.
source: Similar to Fis1 deletion, Tbc1d15 knockdown efficiently blocked mitophagy and decreased LC3 and p62 localization to mitochondria (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 3C-E.

claim: Expression of shRNA-resistant Tbc1d15 in Tbc1d15 knockdown cells restores red puncta formation.
source: Expression of shRNA-resistant Tbc1d15 in these cells restored red puncta formation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Cells knocked down for p62 are deficient for OXPHOS-induced mitophagy.
source: Cells knocked down for p62, as well as p62 knockout cells, were deficient for OXPHOS-induced mitophagy and showed reduced mTurquoise2-LC3B localization to mitochondria (Figure 3C,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 3C,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: p62 knockout cells are deficient for OXPHOS-induced mitophagy.
source: Cells knocked down for p62, as well as p62 knockout cells, were deficient for OXPHOS-induced mitophagy and showed reduced mTurquoise2-LC3B localization to mitochondria (Figure 3C,E; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 3C,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: Expression of mTurquoise2-p62 restores red puncta formation in p62 knockout cells.
source: Expression of mTurquoise2-p62 restored red puncta formation in p62 knockout cells
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Expression of shRNA-resistant p62 restores red puncta formation in p62 shRNA expressing cells.
source: and expression of shRNA-resistant p62 restored red puncta formation in p62 shRNA expressing cells, consistent with a role for P62 in OXPHOS-induced mitophagy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: FIS1 and TBC1D15 are upstream of P62 in promoting autophagic engulfment of mitochondria.
source: Taken together, these results place FIS1 and TBC1D15 upstream of P62 in promoting autophagic engulfment of mitochondria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Pink1-/- cells show a substantial reduction in OXPHOS-induced mitophagy.
source: Pink1-/- cells showed a substantial reduction in OXPHOS-induced mitophagy (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4A-B.

claim: Parkin knockout MEFs have normal mitophagy.
source: However, Parkin knockout MEFs had normal mitophagy (Figure 4A–B)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4A-B.

claim: PINK1 operates upstream of PARKIN.
source: a surprising observation given that PINK1 is known to operate upstream of PARKIN (Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clark et al., 2006; Park et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2006.

claim: MUL1 has been shown to act parallel to the PINK1/PARKIN pathway in ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of mitofusin.
source: Recently, the mitochondrial E3 ligase MUL1 (MULAN/MAPL), has been shown to act parallel to the PINK1/PARKIN pathway in ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of mitofusin (Yun et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yun et al., 2014.

claim: Knockdown of Mul1 in Parkin knockout cells abolishes mitophagy.
source: Indeed, knockdown of Mul1 by either of two independent shRNAs in the Parkin knockout cell abolished mitophagy (Figure 4A–B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4A-B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Knockdown of Mul1 alone does not inhibit mitophagy.
source: In contrast, knockdown of Mul1 alone did not inhibit mitophagy.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: MUL1 and PARKIN have redundant functions in mitophagy.
source: These results reveal that MUL1 and PARKIN have redundant functions in mitophagy.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Inhibition of mitophagy due to loss of PINK1 or PARKIN/MUL1 prevents co-localization of LC3 with mitochondria.
source: Inhibition of mitophagy due to loss of PINK1 or PARKIN/MUL1 prevented co-localization of LC3 with mitochondria (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 4C.

claim: MUL1 and PARKIN have redundant function in mitophagy induced by depolarization of mitochondria with CCCP.
source: We found a similar redundancy of MUL1 and PARKIN function in mitophagy induced by depolarization of mitochondria with CCCP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mitochondria from cells grown in OXPHOS media are ubiquitinated approximately six-fold more than cells grown in glycolytic media.
source: Mitochondria from cells grown in OXPHOS media are ubiquitinated ~six-fold more than cells grown in glycolytic media (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4D,E.

claim: Loss of MUL1 or PARKIN alone has modest or no effect on the induction of mitochondrial ubiquitination under OXPHOS conditions.
source: Loss of MUL1 or PARKIN alone had modest or no effect on the induction of mitochondrial ubiquitination under OXPHOS conditions.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Loss of both MUL1 and PARKIN substantially reduces the ubiquitination of mitochondria under OXPHOS conditions.
source: However, loss of both MUL1 and PARKIN, or PINK1 alone, substantially reduced the ubiquitination of mitochondria (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4D,E.

claim: Loss of PINK1 alone substantially reduces the ubiquitination of mitochondria under OXPHOS conditions.
source: However, loss of both MUL1 and PARKIN, or PINK1 alone, substantially reduced the ubiquitination of mitochondria (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 4D,E.

claim: MUL1 and PARKIN act in concert to ubiquitinate mitochondrial substrates.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that MUL1 and PARKIN act in concert to ubiquitinate mitochondrial substrates
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: A threshold level of ubiquitination may be required to trigger mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions.
source: and that a threshold level of ubiquitination may be required to trigger mitophagy under OXPHOS conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The level of mitochondrial ubiquitination dynamically regulates mitophagy.
source: The level of mitochondrial ubiquitination is known to dynamically regulate mitophagy (Bingol et al., 2014; Cornelissen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bingol et al., 2014 and Cornelissen et al., 2014.

claim: Embryos expressing shRNA against p62 show strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss.
source: We found that embryos expressing shRNA against p62, Tbc1d15, or Pink1 showed strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss, compared to embryos expressing a non-targeting shRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Embryos expressing shRNA against Tbc1d15 show strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss.
source: We found that embryos expressing shRNA against p62, Tbc1d15, or Pink1 showed strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss, compared to embryos expressing a non-targeting shRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 5A.

claim: Embryos expressing shRNA against Pink1 show strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss.
source: We found that embryos expressing shRNA against p62, Tbc1d15, or Pink1 showed strong suppression of paternal mitochondrial loss, compared to embryos expressing a non-targeting shRNA (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 5A.

claim: When p62, Tbc1d15, or Pink1 are knocked down, the majority of embryos retain substantial paternal mitochondria at 84 hr post-fertilization.
source: When these mitophagy genes were knocked down, the majority of embryos retained substantial paternal mitochondria at 84 hr post-fertilization (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 5B.

claim: Less than 20% of embryos containing non-targeting shRNA retain significant paternal mitochondria at 84 hr post-fertilization.
source: In contrast, less than 20% of embryos containing non-targeting shRNA retained significant paternal mitochondria, with the majority of embryos showing complete loss of paternal mitochondria.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Depletion of either Parkin or Mul1 alone modestly reduces paternal mitochondrial elimination.
source: Depletion of either Parkin or Mul1 alone modestly reduced paternal mitochondrial elimination
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Depletion of both Parkin and Mul1 has a severe and highly significant effect on paternal mitochondrial elimination.
source: but depletion of both had a severe and highly significant effect.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Over 60% of Parkin/Mul1-depleted embryos show retention of paternal mitochondria at 84 hr.
source: Over 60% of Parkin/Mul1-depleted embryos showed retention of paternal mitochondria at 84 hr (Figure 5A–B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 5A-B and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Retroviral overexpression of cytosolic FIS1-DN protein in MEFs strongly inhibits OXPHOS-induced mitophagy.
source: Retroviral overexpression of the cytosolic FIS1-DN protein in MEFs strongly inhibits OXPHOS-induced mitophagy (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: When FIS1-DN is expressed in embryos, loss of paternal mitochondria is strongly inhibited.
source: When FIS1-DN was expressed in embryos, we found that loss of paternal mitochondria was strongly inhibited, with the majority retaining substantial paternal mitochondria (Figure 5C–D, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 5C-D and Figure 5—source data 1.

claim: Sperm isolated from the caudal epididymis of PhAM male mice show robust TMRE staining, indicating intact mitochondrial membrane potential.
source: Using the cationic dye TMRE (tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester), we found robust staining of sperm isolated from the caudal epididymis of PhAM male mice, indicating intact mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 6A.

claim: At 18 hr after fertilization, paternal mitochondria remain in a linear cluster in the embryo and stain robustly with TMRE.
source: At 18 hr after fertilization, paternal mitochondria remained in a linear cluster in the embryo and stained robustly with TMRE.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: Over 36 hr following 18 hr post-fertilization, paternal mitochondria gradually lose TMRE staining.
source: However, over the next 36 hr, paternal mitochondria gradually lost TMRE staining, such that at 48 hr and later, nearly all paternal mitochondria failed to stain with TMRE (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 6B-C.

claim: At 48 hr and later post-fertilization, nearly all paternal mitochondria fail to stain with TMRE.
source: However, over the next 36 hr, paternal mitochondria gradually lost TMRE staining, such that at 48 hr and later, nearly all paternal mitochondria failed to stain with TMRE (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figures 6B-C.

claim: Maternal mitochondria always maintain TMRE staining.
source: In the same experiment, maternal mitochondria always maintained TMRE staining
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.

claim: There is selective loss of membrane potential in paternal mitochondria.
source: indicating that there is selective loss of membrane potential in paternal mitochondria
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: At 60 hr post-fertilization, the photo-converted signal in maternally labeled embryos spreads widely into other mitochondria.
source: At 60 hr post-fertilization, the photo-converted signal in maternally labeled embryos had spread widely into other mitochondria, resulting in a dramatic reduction in mean pixel intensity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The photo-converted signal from paternal mitochondria does not diffuse and does not undergo fusion with other mitochondria in the embryo.
source: In contrast, the photo-converted signal from paternal mitochondria did not diffuse and clearly did not undergo fusion with other mitochondria in the embryo.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the study.
